clue.text: Rising pressure one points to at first

indicators.note: at first says the pieces before it go at the front, ahead of the word for pressure

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
N and S are compass points, north and south
urgency is pressure, as in the pressure of a deadline

explanation.surface: A gauge reading of rising pressure that someone points to at the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' brings the one and the points to the front, though 'pressure' leads in the clue; 'to' is only a link. 'Rising' reads as climbing but means a revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: A rising is a revolt or uprising, which is what a rebellion against authority amounts to.

clue.text: Got one's teeth into a little number

parts.note: a bit is a little, a small amount
ten is a number

explanation.surface: Someone chewed into a small number of things.
explanation.definitionFit: Past participle of bite: having closed the jaws on something.

clue.text: Each contains a prime variety of apple

indicators.note: contains says the word for each holds the next piece inside it

parts.note: per means each, as in ten pounds per head
main means prime or principal, as in the main reason

explanation.surface: Each case holds a top-grade apple variety.
explanation.definitionFit: Pearmain names an old English variety of eating apple, such as the Worcester sort.

clue.text: Musical, one originally not recorded right

indicators.note: originally points to the very start of the word one, taking only its opening letter

parts.note: a live performance is one not recorded in advance

explanation.surface: A musical in which one number was originally not recorded properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' does not give I here: 'originally' takes just its first letter, O.
explanation.definitionFit: A stage show by Lionel Bart, based on Dickens's novel about the workhouse orphan.

clue.text: Runs into tedious situation on island before one gets to Italian port

indicators.note: into says the abbreviation for runs goes inside the word for a tedious situation

parts.note: a bind is a tedious, irksome situation
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in a dull situation on an island before reaching an Italian harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: A BIND is British slang for a nuisance or chore; 'before one gets to' puts I last.
explanation.definitionFit: Brindisi is a harbour town in Apulia, on the heel of Italy.

clue.text: Sore in part of chest yesterday

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A soreness felt in part of the chest the day before.
explanation.definitionFit: A small inflamed swelling on the eyelid, a type of painful spot.

clue.text: Against a new thing getting sent back

indicators.note: getting sent back says the word for thing is turned round

parts.note: it can mean a thing, as in 'that's it'

explanation.surface: Opposition to a novelty being returned.
explanation.definitionFit: Anti is a preposition meaning opposed to.

clue.text: I relax, with Thea about to cheer up

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so the letters of the words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tells Thea they will relax with her in order to lift her spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges IRELAX and THEA together; 'with' and 'to' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhilarate is to make someone lively and elated, raising their spirits.

clue.text: Ill-disposed person?

parts.note: read literally, someone disposed, or inclined, to think they are ill, not someone unfriendly

explanation.surface: An unfriendly, hostile individual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ill-disposed' normally means unfriendly; split it to read as inclined towards illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who constantly worries, without cause, that they have a disease.

clue.text: Spread over and lay it on thick

parts.note: to butter bread is to spread it
up can mean over or finished, as in 'time is up'

explanation.surface: Instructions to spread butter generously over toast.
explanation.definitionFit: To flatter someone heavily is to pile on praise to win favour.

clue.text: Surface tack holding points together

indicators.note: holding says the word for tack contains the next piece

parts.note: to tack is to change course at sea, to veer
N and E are compass points, north and east

explanation.surface: Surface tacks pinning things together.
explanation.definitionFit: A veneer is a thin decorative layer over cheaper material, its outer face.

clue.text: Foreign commander's object in constructing programme

indicators.note: in says the word for object goes inside the commander's title

parts.note: an aga is a commander or chief officer in the Ottoman Empire
an end is an object or aim, as in 'to that end'

explanation.surface: A foreign general's aim when drawing up a plan of action.
explanation.definitionFit: A list of items to be dealt with, a schedule for a meeting.

clue.text: Sulky air

explanation.surface: A moody tune.
explanation.definitionFit: A sulky is a light two-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle; air also means bearing or deportment, how one holds oneself.

clue.text: Cruel agent's dealt with in a relative sense

indicators.note: dealt with suggests cards being dealt, so these letters are shuffled

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: A harsh agent has been handled in a way that relates to something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a sense' is linking phrasing round the definition 'relative'.
explanation.definitionFit: The brother of a grandparent is a family member two generations up.

clue.text: No way out for Leo in New York crash

indicators.note: a crash smashes things up, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A traffic accident in New York means Leo cannot get out.
explanation.definitionFit: An emphatic refusal, meaning certainly not.

clue.text: Bill's about to occupy public seat

parts.note: a tab is a bill, as in picking up the tab

indicators.note: to occupy says the word for about sits inside the word for public

parts.note: out means public, known to all, as in 'the secret is out'
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A bill is set to occupy a public bench.
explanation.definitionFit: A tabouret is a low stool without a back.

clue.text: Told off try again with director

parts.note: to re-prove is to prove again, testing once more

explanation.surface: Someone scolded and made to have another go by the director.
explanation.definitionFit: To be reproved is to be rebuked or scolded.

clue.text: Food item produced on the Sussex coast, say?

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: Rye is a town near the Sussex coast, so something raised there is Rye-bred

explanation.surface: A food product made in a seaside part of Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: RYE is a small town in East Sussex, in southern England; something bred there would be Rye-bred.
explanation.definitionFit: A loaf made with rye flour, a type of baked staple.

clue.text: Bearing away substantial number

indicators.note: away says the bearing is taken out of the word for substantial

parts.note: weighty means substantial, heavy
W, west, is a compass bearing

explanation.surface: A course set away from a large number.
explanation.definitionFit: Eighty is a whole number, eight tens.

clue.text: European in bother about overseas currency

indicators.note: in says the abbreviation for European goes inside the word for bother

parts.note: a pest is a bother, a nuisance
a is an abbreviation for about, as in a dating

explanation.surface: A European in trouble over foreign money.
explanation.definitionFit: The peseta was Spain's monetary unit before the euro.

clue.text: Pole's laid back about hard exercise

parts.note: S is the south pole

indicators.note: about says the word for laid back goes round the abbreviation for hard

parts.note: cool means laid back, relaxed
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A Polish man is relaxed about strenuous training.
explanation.definitionFit: To school someone is to train or drill them.

clue.text: Officer's obsession involving king in German city

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for commanding officer

indicators.note: involving says the word for obsession wraps round the abbreviation for king

parts.note: a bug is an obsession, as in the travel bug
R is the abbreviation for king, from Latin rex

explanation.surface: An officer's fixation includes a monarch in a German town.
explanation.definitionFit: Coburg is a town in Bavaria, seat of the Saxe-Coburg dukes.

clue.text: Still available free

explanation.surface: Something remains on offer at no cost.
explanation.definitionFit: A position still to be filled is unfilled and up for grabs; open also means unrestricted, without barriers.

clue.text: Smooth worker displays rigorous control

parts.note: to iron clothes is to smooth them
a hand is a worker, as in a farm hand

explanation.surface: A worker who smooths things out shows strict control.
explanation.definitionFit: Firm, unyielding rule, as in governing with an iron hand.

clue.text: Plant container?

parts.note: reads as a flowerpot, but means the part of a flower's stalk that bears its parts, as well as any holder

explanation.surface: A pot for growing something in.
explanation.walkthrough: Botanists name the swollen tip of a flower stalk, which bears the petals, with this word for a holder.
explanation.definitionFit: Any vessel or holder for something, and in botany the stalk tip bearing a flower.

clue.text: Struggles, failing to open paint

indicators.note: failing to open says the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: toils means struggles, labours

explanation.surface: Someone struggles because the paint tin will not open.
explanation.definitionFit: Oils are oil paints, as in a painting done in oils.
